mainTopic: Understanding as true wealth, how illness affects a person, death by Heaven's decree, and which sick people to visit
overview: The גמרא explains the פסוק 'בחוסר כל' (in want of all things) from the curses in דברים. Several אמוראים and a ברייתא each say what the exile will lack. אביי and the scholars of ארץ ישראל agree with רב נחמן that the worst poverty is lacking דעה (understanding). The גמרא then turns to sickness. It teaches that a sick person recovers only once his sins are forgiven, that he returns to his youth, and that illness can make him forget his learning. Two stories show this: אביי restores רב יוסף's learning, and רבי חייא, with help from a launderer, restores רבי's learning. More teachings follow: healing is a greater miracle than the fiery furnace, and when a person's time comes, everything becomes God's messenger, shown by two stories of strange deaths. Finally, שמואל rules that we visit only sick people with a fever, because talking helps a fever but harms eye and head patients. רבא's comment on fever continues on the next עמוד.

steps.title: רב explains 'in want of all things' as no lamp and no table
steps.stepSummary: After finishing the list of an exile's gear, the גמרא quotes the פסוק 'בחוסר כל', and רב explains it as having no lamp and no table.
steps.simpleTranslation: …and a rug. 'In want of all things': רבי אמי said in the name of רב: without a lamp and without a table.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the list of things an exile takes with him. Then it starts explaining what the פסוק means when it says the exiled people will be 'in want of all things.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says the exile will lack 'everything,' but that is too vague, so the אמוראים try to pin down what it really means. רב gives a practical answer: no light in the house and no table to eat on.

keyTerms.meaning: A rug or mat, which an exile can roll up and carry
In want of all things, a phrase from the curses in דברים

phrases.english: and a rug.
"In want of all things":
Rabbi Ami said in the name of Rav:
without a lamp and without a table.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the earlier list of exile items, then opens a new explanation of a פסוק about exile.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'In want of all things' means without a lamp and without a table.

steps.title: Other אמוראים: no wife, no attendant, no understanding
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא, רב ששת and רב נחמן each give a different meaning for what the exile will lack.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said: without a wife. רב ששת said: without an attendant. רב נחמן said: without understanding.
steps.whatsHappening: Three more אמוראים each offer their own idea of what 'lacking everything' really means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each view points to a different kind of loss. רב חסדא means losing family and companionship, רב ששת means losing help and service, and רב נחמן means losing understanding of the mind. רב נחמן's answer is the one the גמרא will soon back up.

phrases.english: Rav Chisda said: without a wife.
Rav Sheshet said: without an attendant.
Rav Nachman said: without understanding.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers alternative readings of the same פסוק that רב explained in step 1.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'In want of all things' means no wife (רב חסדא), no attendant (רב ששת), or no understanding (רב נחמן).

steps.title: A ברייתא: without salt and without fat
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא explains 'in want of all things' as having no salt and no fat to dip bread in.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: without salt and without fat.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא with one more explanation: the exile will not even have salt or fat for his bread.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the most basic level of poverty, lacking even the simplest things that make plain bread edible.

keyTerms.meaning: It was taught, introducing a ברייתא

phrases.english: It was taught: without salt
and without fat.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another explanation of the same פסוק, this time from a ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'In want of all things' means without salt and without fat.

steps.title: אביי: true poverty is lacking understanding
steps.stepSummary: אביי reports a tradition that the only truly poor person is one who lacks דעה, which backs רב נחמן.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: We have a tradition that a poor person is only one who lacks understanding.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי shares a tradition that supports רב נחמן: real poverty is a lack of understanding.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Out of all the views, אביי backs the one about the mind. Lacking money or things is not real poverty compared with lacking understanding.

keyTerms.meaning: We hold, we have a tradition

phrases.english: Abaye said: We have a tradition:
A poor person is only one lacking in understanding.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רב נחמן's view from step 2.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The only truly poor person is one who lacks understanding.

steps.title: In the West: whoever has understanding has everything
steps.stepSummary: The scholars of ארץ ישראל say that a person with דעה has everything, and a person without it has nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: In ארץ ישראל they say: Whoever has this has everything. Whoever does not have this, what does he have? If he acquired this, what is he missing? If he did not acquire this, what has he acquired?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a saying from ארץ ישראל that makes the same point even stronger: understanding is worth more than everything else.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The saying comes in two pairs. With understanding, nothing else is really missing. Without it, nothing else a person owns really counts. This closes the discussion of 'in want of all things.'

keyTerms.meaning: In the West, meaning ארץ ישראל

steps.whatToRemember: Among all the meanings of 'in want of all things,' the גמרא backs רב נחמן: the worst lack is lacking דעה, because a person with understanding has everything and a person without it has nothing.

phrases.english: In the West they say:
One who has this in him has everything in him.
phrases.notes: 'This' means דעה, the understanding that אביי just talked about.

phrases.english: One who does not have this in him, what is in him?
If he acquired this, what is he lacking?
If he did not acquire this, what has he acquired?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Strengthens אביי's point with a saying from ארץ ישראל.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Understanding is everything: with it nothing is missing, and without it nothing else counts.

steps.title: A sick person recovers only once his sins are forgiven
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלכסנדרי quotes רבי חייא בר אבא: a sick person gets up from his illness only after all his sins are forgiven, based on a פסוק in תהלים.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלכסנדרי said in the name of רבי חייא בר אבא: A sick person does not get up from his illness until all his sins are forgiven, as it says: 'Who forgives all your sins, Who heals all your diseases.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic about sickness. It teaches that healing comes only after forgiveness.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof is the order of the פסוק: first 'forgives all your sins,' then 'heals all your diseases.' So forgiveness comes first, and healing follows.

keyTerms.meaning: As it says, introducing a פסוק

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי אֲלֶכְּסַנְדְּרִי אָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא:
phrases.english: Rabbi Alexandri said in the name of Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba:
A sick person does not get up from his illness

phrases.aramaic: עַד שֶׁמּוֹחֲלִין לוֹ עַל כֹּל עֲוֹנוֹתָיו,
phrases.english: until they forgive him for all his sins,
as it says: "Who forgives all your sins,
Who heals all your diseases."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אֲלֶכְּסַנְדְּרִי אָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic about sickness and recovery.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Recovery from illness comes only after all of a person's sins are forgiven.

steps.title: רב המנונא: the healed person returns to his youth
steps.stepSummary: רב המנונא teaches that a person who recovers goes back to the days of his youth, based on a פסוק in איוב.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב המנונא said: He returns to the days of his youth, as it says: 'His flesh becomes fresher than a child's; he returns to the days of his youth.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב המנונא adds what happens once a sick person recovers: he becomes young and fresh again.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This builds on the previous step. The sick person is not only healed. His body is renewed, as the פסוק in איוב describes.

phrases.aramaic: רַב הַמְנוּנָא אָמַר: חוֹזֵר לִימֵי עֲלוּמָיו,
phrases.english: Rav Hamnuna said: He returns to the days of his youth,
phrases.notes: He is talking about the sick person who has just recovered.

phrases.english: as it says: "His flesh is fresher than a child's;
he returns to the days of his youth."

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב הַמְנוּנָא אָמַר: חוֹזֵר לִימֵי עֲלוּמָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds what happens after the recovery described in step 6.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person who recovers from illness returns to the freshness of his youth.

steps.title: רב יוסף: illness makes a person forget his learning
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף explains the פסוק 'You overturned all his lying down in his illness' to mean that a sick person forgets his learning.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'You overturned all his lying down in his illness.' רב יוסף said: This means that he forgets his learning.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף explains a פסוק in תהלים about illness. He says sickness can turn a person's learning upside down so that he forgets it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יוסף reads 'overturned' as describing what illness does to a person's mind: what he had in order gets turned over and lost. This sets up the story in the next step, where it happens to רב יוסף himself.

phrases.english: "You overturned all his lying down in his illness":
Rav Yosef said:
This is to say that he forgets his learning.

steps.triggerLanguage: כׇּל מִשְׁכָּבוֹ הָפַכְתָּ בְחׇלְיוֹ, אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the topic of illness with another effect it has on a person.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Illness can cause a person to forget his Torah learning.

steps.title: רב יוסף falls ill, and אביי restores his learning
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף became sick and forgot his learning, and his student אביי taught it back to him.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף became ill and his learning was uprooted from him. אביי reviewed it back in front of him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story: what רב יוסף said about illness happened to him, and אביי helped him get his learning back.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי had learned from רב יוסף, so he could review that material with his teacher and restore what had been forgotten. The teacher ended up relearning his own Torah from his student.

phrases.english: Rav Yosef became ill,
his learning was uprooted from him,
Abaye restored it before him.
phrases.notes: אביי went over with רב יוסף what he had learned from him, until רב יוסף had it back.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows רב יוסף's teaching from step 8 happening in his own life.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב יוסף forgot his learning through illness, and אביי restored it.

steps.title: This explains the repeated 'I never heard this' exchange
steps.stepSummary: The story explains why, all over the תלמוד, רב יוסף says he never heard a teaching and אביי answers that רב יוסף taught it to them himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what we say everywhere: רב יוסף said, 'I never heard this teaching,' and אביי said to him, 'You told it to us, and from this ברייתא you told it to us.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא ties the story to a common exchange in the תלמוד and explains where it comes from.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Many times in שס, רב יוסף does not recognize a teaching, and אביי reminds him that he himself taught it. This story gives the background: רב יוסף had forgotten his learning in his illness, so אביי had to remind him of his own teachings and their sources.

keyTerms.meaning: A ברייתא, a teaching from the time of the תנאים

steps.whatToRemember: Illness can make a person forget his learning. That happened to רב יוסף, and it explains why אביי often reminds him, 'You taught it to us, and from this ברייתא.'
steps.confusionAlert: רב יוסף is not disagreeing with his own teaching when he says 'I never heard this.' He simply forgot it because of his illness, and אביי is reminding him.
steps.whyThisMatters: It explains a pattern that shows up again and again in the תלמוד between רב יוסף and אביי.

phrases.english: This is what we say everywhere:

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף: לָא שְׁמִיעַ לִי הָדָא שְׁמַעְתָּא,
phrases.english: Rav Yosef said: I have not heard this teaching,

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ אַבָּיֵי: אַתְּ אַמְרִיתַהּ נִיהֲלַן,
phrases.english: Abaye said to him: You said it to us,
and from this baraita you said it to us.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the story from step 9 to explain a repeated exchange in the תלמוד.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The common exchange where רב יוסף forgets a teaching and אביי reminds him comes from רב יוסף's illness, which made him forget his learning.

steps.title: רבי forgets his learning and רבי חייא recovers it
steps.stepSummary: רבי taught רבי חייא seven of thirteen aspects of a הלכה. When רבי got sick and forgot them, רבי חייא restored the seven, and recovered the other six from a launderer who had overheard רבי.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רבי learned thirteen aspects of a הלכה, he taught seven of them to רבי חייא. Later רבי got sick and forgot them. רבי חייא taught him back the seven, but six were lost. A launderer used to overhear רבי studying them, so רבי חייא learned them from the launderer and taught them back to רבי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a second story, like the one about רב יוסף, where a great teacher forgets his learning when he is sick and gets it back from others.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This story backs up רב יוסף's teaching that a sick person forgets his learning. It adds a new detail: what רבי never taught anyone was saved only because a simple launderer happened to overhear him.

phrases.english: When Rebbi would learn
thirteen aspects of a halacha,
he taught Rabbi Chiya seven of them.
In the end, Rebbi became sick,
Rabbi Chiya brought back before him
those seven aspects that he had taught him,
but six were gone.
There was a certain launderer
who used to hear Rebbi
when he was studying them.

phrases.aramaic: אֲזַל רַבִּי חִיָּיא וּגְמַר יָתְהוֹן קַמֵּי קַצָּרָא
phrases.english: Rabbi Chiya went and learned them from the launderer
and came and brought them back before Rebbi.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי הֲוָה גְּמִיר רַבִּי תְּלָת עֶשְׂרֵי אַפֵּי הִילְכָתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel story to רב יוסף and אביי, showing again that illness makes a person forget his learning.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Even רבי forgot his learning through illness; what he had taught others, or what others had overheard, could be brought back to him.

steps.title: רבי thanks the launderer: 'You made me'
steps.stepSummary: When רבי saw the launderer, he told him that he had 'made' both him and רבי חייא. Another version says רבי told him that he made רבי חייא, and רבי חייא made רבי.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whenever רבי saw that launderer, he said to him: You made me and חייא. Some say he said: You made חייא, and חייא made me.
steps.whatsHappening: The story ends with רבי praising the launderer, and the גמרא gives two versions of what he said.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both versions give the launderer credit for saving the lost learning. The first says he helped both רבי and רבי חייא directly. The second sees a chain: the launderer taught רבי חייא, and רבי חייא then taught רבי.

keyTerms.meaning: you made me (you made me who I am)

steps.whatToRemember: Even a simple person who helps bring back Torah learning is treated as having 'made' the great scholars who regained it.

phrases.aramaic: כַּד הֲוָה חָזֵי לֵיהּ רַבִּי לְהָהוּא קַצָּרָא
phrases.english: When Rebbi would see that launderer,
Rebbi said to him:
You made me and Chiya.
phrases.notes: He means: thanks to you, both of us got back the learning that would have been lost.

phrases.english: Some say this is what he said to him:
You made Chiya,
and Chiya made me.

steps.triggerLanguage: כַּד הֲוָה חָזֵי לֵיהּ רַבִּי לְהָהוּא קַצָּרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the story from the last step with רבי's words to the launderer, in two versions.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי credited the launderer with 'making' him and רבי חייא, either directly or through רבי חייא.

steps.title: Healing a sick person is a greater miracle than the fiery furnace
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלכסנדרי quotes רבי חייא בר אבא: the miracle of a sick person recovering is greater than the miracle of חנניה מישאל ועזריה, because their fire was man-made but a fever is a fire from Heaven.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלכסנדרי said in the name of רבי חייא בר אבא: The miracle done for a sick person is greater than the one done for חנניה מישאל ועזריה. Their fire was made by people, and anyone can put it out. But the fire of a sick person comes from Heaven, and who can put that out?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to רבי אלכסנדרי's teachings about sick people (like step 6) and adds another one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The comparison is about who made the fire. A man-made fire can be put out by people, but a fever is sent by Heaven, so only Heaven can 'put it out.' That makes recovery a bigger miracle.

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רַבִּי אֲלֶכְּסַנְדְּרִי אָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא:
phrases.english: And Rabbi Alexandri said that Rabbi Chiya bar Abba said:
Greater is the miracle done for a sick person

phrases.aramaic: יוֹתֵר מִן הַנֵּס שֶׁנַּעֲשָׂה לַחֲנַנְיָה מִישָׁאֵל וַעֲזַרְיָה.
phrases.english: than the miracle done for Chananya, Mishael, and Azarya.

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁל חֲנַנְיָה מִישָׁאֵל וַעֲזַרְיָה אֵשׁ שֶׁל הֶדְיוֹט,
phrases.english: That of Chananya, Mishael, and Azarya was an ordinary person's fire,
and anyone can put it out.

phrases.aramaic: וְזוֹ שֶׁל חוֹלֶה — שֶׁל שָׁמַיִם הִיא,
phrases.english: But this one of a sick person is from Heaven,
phrases.notes: The 'fire' of a sick person is his fever.

phrases.english: and who can put it out?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי אֲלֶכְּסַנְדְּרִי אָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the stories, the גמרא returns to the series of רבי אלכסנדרי's teachings about illness.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A sick person's recovery is a greater miracle than surviving the fiery furnace, because a fever is a fire from Heaven.

steps.title: When a person's time has come, everything rules over him
steps.stepSummary: Once the end of a person's life arrives, everything can harm him, learned from קין's words 'whoever finds me will kill me.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלכסנדרי said in the name of רבי חייא בר אבא, and some say רבי יהושע בן לוי said: Once a person's end has come, everything has power over him, as it says: 'Whoever finds me will kill me.'
steps.whatsHappening: Another teaching from the same series: when Heaven decides a person's time is up, anything can become the cause of his death.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof is from קין, who feared that after God's judgment against him, anyone he met could kill him. The teaching moves from sickness and healing to the time of death itself.

keyTerms.meaning: and some say it in the name of (a different speaker)
a person's end, his time to die
rule over him, have power over him

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רַבִּי אֲלֶכְּסַנְדְּרִי אָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא
phrases.english: And Rabbi Alexandri said that Rabbi Chiya bar Abba said,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמְרִי לַהּ אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי:
phrases.english: and some say Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said:
Once a person's end has arrived,
everything has power over him,
as it says: 'Whoever finds me will kill me.'
phrases.notes: בראשית 4:14. קין says this after God punishes him.

steps.triggerLanguage: כֵּיוָן שֶׁהִגִּיעַ קִיצּוֹ שֶׁל אָדָם הַכֹּל מוֹשְׁלִים בּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the series of teachings by רבי אלכסנדרי, now about the time of death.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When a person's time to die has come, anything can harm him; the source is קין's words.

steps.title: רב brings a different פסוק for the same idea
steps.stepSummary: רב learns the same idea from a פסוק in תהלים: 'They stand this day according to Your judgments, for all are Your servants.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said it is learned from this פסוק: 'They stand this day according to Your judgments, for all are Your servants.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב agrees with the idea from the last step but brings a different פסוק as the source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The key words are 'all are Your servants.' When Heaven judges that a person's time is up, everything in the world becomes God's messenger to carry out that judgment.
steps.confusionAlert: רב is not arguing with the idea itself. He agrees that everything has power over a person whose time has come; he only brings a different source for it.

phrases.english: Rav said: from this verse:
'They stand this day according to Your judgments,'
'for all are Your servants.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different פסוק for the same teaching as the last step.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The idea that everything rules over a person whose time has come is learned from 'for all are Your servants.'

steps.title: A tall man dies from a tiny fall
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר שילא was told that a tall man riding a small mule fell off when the mule was frightened at a bridge, and died. רבה בר שילא applied רב's פסוק to him.
steps.simpleTranslation: People told רבה בר שילא: A man died. He was tall and riding a small mule. When he reached a bridge, the mule got frightened, threw him off, and he died. רבה בר שילא read about him: 'They stand this day according to Your judgments.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story that shows the teaching in real life: when someone's time has come, even a tiny fall can kill him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The fall should not have been dangerous, since a tall man on a short mule barely falls at all. רבה בר שילא saw this as proof of רב's פסוק: even a small mule became God's 'servant' to carry out the judgment.
steps.whatToRemember: When Heaven decides a person's time has come, even something harmless, like a short fall from a small mule, can carry out that decree.

phrases.english: They said to Rabba bar Sheila:
A man has died.
He was tall and was riding a small mule,
phrases.notes: The point: he was so tall and the mule so short that the fall was tiny.

phrases.english: when it reached a bridge, it got frightened,
threw him off, and he died.
He read about him: 'They stand this day according to Your judgments.'
phrases.notes: This is the פסוק רב quoted in the last step; רבה בר שילא applies it to the man who died.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבָּה בַּר שֵׁילָא אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ: שְׁכֵיב גַּבְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A story showing רב's פסוק in action.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבה בר שילא applied 'They stand this day according to Your judgments' to a man who died from a harmless-seeming fall.

steps.title: שמואל sees a scorpion ride a frog across a river
steps.stepSummary: שמואל watched a scorpion ride a frog across a river and sting a man to death, and he applied the פסוק 'They stand this day according to Your judgments.'
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל saw a frog with a scorpion sitting on it. The frog crossed the river, the scorpion stung a man, and the man died. שמואל read the פסוק about him: 'They stand this day according to Your judgments.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells one more story showing that when a person's time has come, anything can become God's messenger to kill him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A scorpion cannot cross a river on its own, so it needed the frog to carry it. Because both animals worked together to reach this man, שמואל saw them as God's servants carrying out a judgment. This is the same פסוק רב used in Step 15 and רבה בר שילא used in Step 16.

keyTerms.meaning: He read (a פסוק) about him, meaning he applied the פסוק to this case

steps.whatToRemember: Once a person's end arrives, even a frog and a scorpion become God's messengers. This closes the teaching that began in Step 14 and the two stories that illustrate it.

phrases.english: Shmuel saw a certain frog
and that a scorpion was sitting on the frog
and it crossed the river
The scorpion stung a man, and he died.
He read about him: 'They stand this day according to Your judgments.'
phrases.notes: תהלים 119:91. It is the same פסוק רב quoted in Step 15.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second story that illustrates רב's פסוק, parallel to רבה בר שילא's story in Step 16.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Animals can act as God's agents to carry out a person's death when his time has come.

steps.title: Visit only a sick person who has a fever
steps.stepSummary: שמואל rules that one visits a sick person only if fever has overcome him.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל said: We visit a sick person only if he is someone whom fever has overcome.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic: a rule from שמואל about which sick people should be visited.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל limits the מצוה of visiting to people with a fever. The wording 'only' tells us some other illnesses are left out. The next steps work out which ones and why.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל: אֵין מְבַקְּרִין אֶת הַחוֹלֶה
phrases.english: Shmuel said: We do not visit a sick person
except one whom fever has overcome.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל: אֵין מְבַקְּרִין אֶת הַחוֹלֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the stories to a new topic, the laws of visiting the sick.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Visiting the sick applies only to a patient with a fever.

steps.title: What does שמואל's rule leave out?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which illnesses שמואל's word 'only' comes to exclude.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does this come to exclude?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a short question to set up the next step: which sick people is שמואל telling us not to visit?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying 'only a fever patient' does not explain itself. The גמרא wants to know which specific illnesses שמואל meant to exclude.

keyTerms.meaning: To exclude what? (the question of what a rule leaves out)

phrases.english: What does it come to exclude?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the scope of שמואל's rule.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which illnesses are excluded by שמואל's word 'only.'

steps.title: Excluded: stomach, eye, and head illnesses
steps.stepSummary: שמואל's rule excludes the illnesses listed in a ברייתא: stomach illness, eye illness, and headaches.
steps.simpleTranslation: It comes to exclude what was taught in a ברייתא: רבי יוסי בן פרטא says in the name of רבי אליעזר: We do not visit people with stomach illness, people with eye illness, or people with headaches.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by quoting a ברייתא that lists three kinds of patients one should not visit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל's 'only' points to the cases in this ברייתא. Stomach, eye, and head patients are left out of the מצוה of visiting.

keyTerms.meaning: That it was taught in a ברייתא
People with stomach or intestinal illness

phrases.english: To exclude that which was taught:

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בֶּן פְּרָטָא אוֹמֵר מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei ben Perata says in the name of Rabbi Eliezer:
We do not visit people with stomach illness,

phrases.aramaic: וְלֹא חוֹלֵי הָעַיִן וְלֹא מְחוּשֵׁי הָרֹאשׁ.
phrases.english: nor people with eye illness, nor people with headaches.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 19.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The rule excludes stomach patients, eye patients, and headache sufferers, as listed in רבי יוסי בן פרטא's ברייתא.

steps.title: Why not visit eye and headache patients?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא understands why stomach patients are not visited, because they would be embarrassed, but asks what the reason is for eye and head patients.
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes sense that we do not visit stomach patients, because of embarrassment. But what is the reason for eye patients and headache patients?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא accepts the reason for one case on the list and asks for the reason behind the other two.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A stomach patient may need the bathroom often, so a visitor would embarrass him. Eye and head illnesses have no such problem, so the גמרא needs a different reason for leaving them out.

phrases.english: Granted, stomach patients are not visited because of embarrassment.
But eye patients and headache sufferers,
what is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reasoning behind part of the ברייתא quoted in Step 20.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why eye patients and headache sufferers should not be visited.

steps.title: Talking hurts the eye but helps a fever
steps.stepSummary: The reason comes from רב יהודה: speaking is bad for the eye and good for a fever.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is because of what רב יהודה said. רב יהודה said: Speaking is harmful for the eye and beneficial for a fever.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question with רב יהודה's rule about the effects of talking.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A visitor makes the patient talk. For eye and head patients, talking causes harm, so visiting them hurts them. For a fever patient, talking helps, which fits שמואל's rule in Step 18 to visit fever patients.
steps.whatToRemember: We visit fever patients because talking helps them. We do not visit stomach patients because of embarrassment, or eye and head patients because talking harms them.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not read קַשְׁיָא here as the usual word for a challenge in the גמרא. Here it simply means 'harmful.'

phrases.english: It is because of what Rav Yehuda said,
as Rav Yehuda said:
Speaking is harmful for the eye
and beneficial for a fever.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִשּׁוּם דְּרַב יְהוּדָה, דְּאָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 21.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Visitors make the patient speak, and speaking harms eye and head patients but helps fever patients.

steps.title: רבא: fever would be helpful if not for the Angel of Death
steps.stepSummary: רבא begins a statement that fever would be beneficial, if not for its role as the messenger of the מלאך המות.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: This fever, if it were not the messenger of the מלאך המות, would be beneficial...
steps.whatsHappening: רבא adds a new comment about fever, continuing the theme of רב יהודה's rule. His statement continues past the end of this section.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא calls fever the agent of the מלאך המות, because it often leads to serious, deadly illness. Apart from that danger, he says, fever would actually be good for a person. His full point continues on the next עמוד.

phrases.english: Rava said: This fever,
if it were not the messenger of the Angel of Death,
it would be beneficial
phrases.notes: רבא's sentence keeps going on the next עמוד.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on רב יהודה's statement that speech is good for a fever, adding a further comment on fever.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Fever would be beneficial if it did not so often lead to death.
